Rosacea

Small uncontrolled clinical reports describe reduced facial redness, flushing, or inflammatory lesions after LED or fluorescence-based treatment. A randomized trial of PBM added to oral minocycline has been published, but accessible records do not report its results. Two mouse studies and one linked keratinocyte experiment found lower inflammatory measures after light exposure.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small uncontrolled clinical reports describe reduced facial redness, flushing, or inflammatory lesions after LED or fluorescence-based treatment. A randomized trial of PBM added to oral minocycline has been published, but accessible records do not report its results. Two mouse studies and one linked keratinocyte experiment found lower inflammatory measures after light exposure.

Summary of the Evidence

Nine publications are assigned to rosacea. They include one randomized clinical trial, one single-arm human study, two case series, one case report, one patient survey, one review, and two mouse studies; one mouse publication also includes cultured-cell experiments. The four uncontrolled clinical reports describe 15 people in total. The randomized trial is a short letter, and the accessible PubMed and publisher pages have no abstract or numerical outcome data. Fluorescent-light-energy studies combine a chromophore gel with blue LED illumination, so they do not test ordinary LED exposure alone.

Human and clinical evidence

The randomized clinical publication studied oral minocycline combined with PBM and is classified as an evaluator-blinded controlled trial. Its accessible records do not report the sample size, comparison details, or results, so the direction or size of any added PBM effect cannot be stated (Su et al. 2023).

A nine-person postmarket study delivered fluorescent light energy once weekly for four weeks. It reported a significant reduction in inflammatory facial erythema, improvements in flushing and redness, and better patient-reported self-perception and emotional well-being. There was no control group, and the intervention used a photoconverter gel with a blue LED platform (Wade et al. 2021).

Two case reports and a three-person case series also described reductions in inflammation or erythema after blue-and-red LED or fluorescence-based treatments. In one case, facial inflammation was markedly lower after four weekly blue-light sessions with a photoconverter gel. These reports show the direction of observed changes, but without control groups they cannot determine how much improvement was caused by light treatment. A patient survey describes views about light and laser therapy but does not measure treatment efficacy.

Animal evidence

In an LL-37-induced mouse model, combined 590-nm amber-yellow visible light and 830-nm near-infrared PBM significantly reduced erythema scores and inflammatory-cell infiltration. The investigators also measured lower expression of inflammatory mediators and the angiogenesis marker CD31, together with changes in immune-cell infiltration (Wu et al. 2022).

A second mouse study found that 630-nm red visible and 940-nm near-infrared LED exposure reduced inflammatory-cell infiltration, blood-vessel dilation, red-cell leakage, and epidermal thickening in rosacea-like skin. The two wavelengths produced similar effects in that model (Lee et al. 2016).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The Lee study also exposed cultured human epidermal keratinocytes to LED light. At 630 and 940 nm, the investigators found lower expression of TLR2, KLK5, and LL-37 and lower protease activity after treatment. No separate ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human reports include blue visible LED at 447 nm, combined blue 480-nm and red 650-nm light, and fluorescence-based protocols using 415- and 447-nm blue LEDs with a chromophore gel. The nine-person postmarket study used weekly sessions for four weeks. In mice, one protocol combined 590-nm amber-yellow visible light at 25 mW with 830-nm near-infrared light at 50 mW, while another used 630-nm red and 940-nm near-infrared exposure three times. The minocycline trial's dosimetry is not accessible. Differences in devices and co-treatments prevent identifying one best wavelength or dose.

Interpretation

The clinical case reports describe lower redness, flushing, and inflammatory lesions, and the nine-person postmarket study reports improvement in erythema and patient-reported outcomes. The randomized minocycline-plus-PBM publication could clarify an adjunctive effect, but its results are not available in the accessible record. The mouse and keratinocyte studies independently show reductions in inflammatory features or markers. Together these findings give a specific basis for further clinical testing, while current human evidence does not yet establish the size or durability of benefit.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for short-term clinical reduction in redness or inflammatory lesions Very low for the added effect of PBM with oral minocycline Low for reduced erythema and inflammatory measures in mouse models
Publications and records9 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Small clinical reports describe lower redness, flushing, or inflammatory lesions, and a randomized adjunctive trial has been published. Its accessible record does not report results or sample size, so it cannot confirm an added benefit from PBM. Mouse and cell experiments also found reduced inflammatory measures. Independent controlled trials with complete outcomes and dose details would support a stronger clinical rating.
